state.misconception_label: Believes if you changed all values by the same proportion the range would not change

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are discussing the \( 5 \) plants with these heights: \( 24 \mathrm{~cm}, 17 \mathrm{~cm}, 42 \mathrm{~cm}, 26 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm} \) Tom says if all the plants were cut in half, the range wouldn't change. Katie says if all the plants grew by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) each, the range wouldn't change. Who do you agree with? I got Only
Tom because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: It seems like you're trying to understand how changing all the values by the same proportion would affect the range. Let's think about how the range is affected when all values are multiplied by a certain factor. Can you describe what happens to the range when all values are cut in half or increased by \(3 \) cm?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Um, okay so like... when you cut all the plants in half, the biggest one and the smallest one both get smaller by the same amount, so the difference between them stays the same? But when you add 3 cm to each plant, they all grow the same, so that doesn't change the difference either... wait, so does that mean both Tom and Katie are right then?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: You're on the right track with your reasoning! Think about how the range is calculated and how changing all values by the same proportion would affect the difference between the largest and smallest values. Can you apply this concept to Tom and Katie's scenarios to determine who is correct?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher fails to address the critical distinction between multiplicative and additive changes, reinforces the student's incorrect reasoning in Turn 2 by saying they're "on the right track," and the student ends more confused than they started, now incorrectly believing both Tom and Katie are right.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher fails to scaffold effectively by not addressing the student's conceptual confusion between multiplicative and additive changes, and instead of breaking down the problem into manageable steps when the student shows confusion in Turn 2, the teacher simply redirects them back to the same question without adjusting support level.
